articles.title: IAMAI seeks GST cut for app-based rides
articles.summary: New Delhi: The app-based mobility industry has pitched for exemption from the 5% goods and services tax (GST), arguing that the levy is being imposed on platforms that often do not collect fares from passengers.In a representation to the government and the Goods and Services Tax Council, the Internet and Mobile Association of India (IAMAI) said the current tax structure does not reflect how several ride-hailing platforms actually operate.On these platforms, a driver collects the fare directly from the passenger and the app acts primarily as a technology platform connecting the two, it said. Yet, the industry body said the platform is required to account for the 5% GST on the value of the ride.The IAMAI said this creates an unfair tax burden that ultimately gets passed on to drivers or passengers.The association made a case for excluding such technology-based platforms from the provision under Section 9(5) of the CGST Act that shifts the GST responsibility for passenger transport services to the digital platform.The industry body also flagged conflicting rulings by state tax authorities on whether such platforms fall under the provision, saying the lack of clarity has left the sector facing prolonged uncertainty.

articles.title: US unemployment claims dip to 206,000
articles.summary: Slightly fewer Americans filed for unemployment claims last week as jobless claims remain at historically low levels and layoffs are still relatively rare.Filings for benefits dipped to 206,000 last week from a revised 207,000 the week before, the Labor Department reported Thursday. The four-week average of claims, which smooths out week-to-week volatility, also fell modestly to 206,000.Claims for jobless benefits are a proxy for layoffs, and economists watch them because they can be a sign of where the job market is headed. For the past year, claims have mostly stayed within a historically low range of 200,000 to 230,000 a week.The American job market has remained sturdy despite higher gasoline prices that have squeezed businesses and consumers since the fighting with Iran began Feb. 28.Layoffs are low. Businesses, remembering the labor shortages that followed the end of pandemic lockdowns, are reluctant to let go of staff. They're hiring - but modestly by the standards of recent years.So far this year, employers - companies, government agencies and nonprofits - have been adding an average 80,000 jobs a month, including a surprising 162,000 in August. That is an improvement on a dismal 2025 when monthly job creation averaged less than 10,000 as high interest rates and President Donald Trump's erratic trade policies discouraged hiring.But it remains well below the 166,000 monthly jobs created, on average, in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns.

articles.title: New India industrial revolution takes shape
articles.summary: New Delhi: India is entering a new phase of industrialisation as rising domestic demand and government support draw private capital into emerging sectors including space, semiconductors, data centres, electronics and solar manufacturing, brokerage Jefferies said in a report.The government has backed the push through measures including opening the space sector to private companies, tax incentives for data centres, large production-linked schemes for semiconductors, electronics and solar, localisation requirements and purchases of GPUs.The resulting investment cycle is creating opportunities not only in end-product manufacturing but also across domestic supply chains, components, infrastructure and engineering services, it said.Also read | Bilats, brush-bys, pull-asides: The secret art of summitry at BRICSOn the space sector, Jefferies said India is among a handful of spacefaring nations with globally competitive capabilities. The government opened the sector to private participation in 2020 and is targeting an almost five-fold expansion of the space economy between 2023 and 2030, to about USD 40 billion-USD 45 billion.Indian startups are increasingly moving from early-stage innovation toward commercial execution. Skyroot is targeting an orbital launch in July, while Pixxel is developing high-resolution earth-observation satellites. Agnikul is working on 3D-printed rocket engines and Digantara is developing satellite-based space-surveillance capabilities.The shift is broadening private-sector participation beyond satellite services into launch vehicles, propulsion, earth observation and space situational awareness.The brokerage said India's semiconductor ambitions are moving from policy planning toward execution, with about USD 20 billion of investments announced or underway, including a chip fabrication plant under construction and several outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) projects moving toward production.A new incentive plan worth about USD 13 billion is expected to further expand the ecosystem and increase domestic value addition, including in chip design.Also read | 7 cases dropped: HDFC scores big win in BahrainSupply-chain depth, availability of skilled talent and competition from established semiconductor hubs remain challenges. But the investment pipeline is laying the foundations for a domestic semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem.On the data-centre industry, it said India has emerged as a strategic digital-infrastructure segment, with co-location capacity rising five-fold over the past five years to about 2 gigawatts.Cloud adoption, digitisation and data-localisation requirements are driving demand. Capacity could expand another five-fold to about 10 GW over the next five years, supported by favourable cost economics, policy measures and rising demand from hyperscalers.That expansion could represent about USD 9 billion in revenue for data-centre operators and roughly USD 45 billion of investment across power, cooling, construction and network infrastructure, according to the report.Jefferies said India's electronics industry is entering a new phase, with policymakers and manufacturers focusing increasingly on domestic value addition and component production.Electronics exports have risen sharply, while schemes including the Electronics Components Manufacturing Scheme (ECMS) and Mobile 2.0 are intended to deepen backward integration and reduce dependence on imports.The report forecasts that ECMS could cover about 50 per cent of the bill of materials for mobile components over the next six years, compared with less than 20 per cent currently.Printed circuit boards, including high-density interconnect and multi-layer boards, are a particular focus. The segment has an estimated USD 5 billion total addressable market, with 85-90 per cent of demand currently met through imports.The brokerage said India has emerged as the world's second-largest solar photovoltaic manufacturer, with about 35 GW of solar-cell capacity operational and another 100 GW under construction.Policy measures including the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM), domestic-content requirements and production-linked incentives are encouraging greater integration across the solar manufacturing chain, including cells, wafers and ingots.The report expects about 90 per cent of the solar manufacturing value chain to be localised by 2030.India is also positioned to benefit from a global supply-demand imbalance in aerospace, leveraging relatively competitive manufacturing costs and its engineering talent pool, it said, adding that Boeing and Airbus already source an estimated USD 1.4-1.6 billion annually from India, while domestic companies including Aequs, Azad, BHFC, DYTC, RW, MOTHERSO and SANSERA are supplying global original-equipment manufacturers and Tier-1 suppliers and expanding their aerospace businesses.The opportunity extends beyond outsourcing into higher-value manufacturing and engineering as global aerospace companies diversify supply chains.The common thread across these industries is a push to move India higher up global supply chains. Government incentives are being combined with a large domestic market, rising digitisation, strategic localisation and growing demand for manufacturing and infrastructure.Space and semiconductors are relatively new areas of private-sector participation, while electronics and solar are moving from import dependence and assembly toward greater domestic value addition. Data centres are emerging as a major infrastructure build-out, and aerospace offers an avenue for Indian manufacturers to capture a larger share of global production.Together, these sectors point to a broader industrial strategy: use India's domestic demand and policy support to build local capabilities, attract private investment and position Indian companies deeper inside global technology and manufacturing supply chains.

articles.title: Kant's 3-step formula for India's BRICS move
articles.summary: India must ensure that the language of the BRICS summit document is progressive and forward-looking, Amitabh Kant, former India G20 Sherpa and former chief executive officer of NITI Aayog, highlighted ahead of the bloc's summit beginning September 11."It is important that we are able to resolve the differences despite the conflict in West Asia. When you have Iran, the UAE and Saudi Arabia, it is highly complex. But India must play a key role in getting the right minimum language to be able to resolve this," Kant said. He added that, apart from the BRICS summit, there would be significant bilateral engagement.Also read: China's Xi Jinping to visit India for first time in seven years as New Delhi hosts BRICS Summit"The Prime Minister will be meeting Putin and Xi Jinping, and the China-India play on issues of development, trade and technology is critical," Kant said at the India Today BRICS Roundtable.Kant said he expected further movement in India-China relations, which had been progressing smoothly before tensions led India to introduce Press Note 3. He also referred to changes in the foreign direct investment framework, saying that beneficial ownership had now been defined under Press Note 3, allowing up to 10% investment by Chinese entities under specified conditions."But we need a movement forward. We need to advance this forward," Kant said.Kant's three step formula:India should push for a progressive, forward-looking BRICS summit document and help bridge differences over West Asia.Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s meetings with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping could drive significant bilateral engagement alongside the summit.India should push for further movement in ties with China, particularly on development, trade and technology.Former NITI Aayog chief said India’s foreign policy has been shaped by a strategy of being “multi-aligned”, allowing it to deepen economic partnerships across competing geopolitical blocs while pursuing its growth ambitions.“To achieve our ambition of economic growth, we have done multiple FTAs. But we also have to work with Russia and China,” Kant said, arguing that India cannot afford to view its economic and strategic relationships through the lens of a single alliance.Also read: BRICS Summit 2026: Stage set at Bharat Mandapam as PM Modi hosts expanded global powerhouseEnergy security will remain a key challenge, he said, particularly as India pursues its ambition of becoming a developed economy. India will continue to require fossil fuel imports for the foreseeable future, with energy purchases adding pressure on the rupee and affecting the broader economy.Kant also flagged the strategic implications of developments in West Asia, saying that if the US were to succeed in controlling Iranian crude, it could potentially gain majority influence over a significant share of the world's fossil fuel resources.India will therefore need to navigate its relationships with major powers carefully, including the US and China, while safeguarding its energy and economic interests, he said.On China, Kant said Beijing's economic model remains heavily focused on exports rather than imports, while its domestic market continues to be marked by non-tariff barriers.India should use bilateral discussions with China to press for the transfer of clean-energy technologies to other BRICS partners, Kant said. He argued that China's dominance over critical clean-energy technologies had become a strategic concern, with Beijing increasingly “weaponising” its technological capabilities.“We do a very substantial amount of imports from China. It's very important to understand that China is weaponising all its new technologies,” Kant said.He highlighted this should also be a key issue during PM Modi's bilateral engagement with Chinese President Xi Jinping. India, he said, must understand the implications of China's control over clean-energy supply chains, particularly technologies such as batteries, where concentrated market power can influence prices.Kant said India must simultaneously strengthen its own technological capabilities. He pointed to the opening up of key sectors such as geospatial services, drones and space, along with India's push into cutting-edge technologies including semiconductors, as two major developments.These initiatives could give India “quantum growth”, he said.As India gears up to host BRICS, Kant said the country should focus its agenda on trade, investment, development and climate issues. BRICS nations account for a significant share of global trade, and greater cooperation could benefit economies across the Global South, he added.A key lesson from India's G20 presidency, according to Kant, is the importance of building consensus through multilateral negotiations. Achieving consensus should be the hallmark of India's BRICS presidency as well, he said, particularly given the expansion of the grouping and the differing interests of its members.At the same time, Kant stressed the importance of India's relationship with the US.“No country has made wealth without working with the US,” he said, arguing that India must act as a “mature, seasoned player” capable of steering through increasingly turbulent geopolitical conditions.India's ability to build consensus among countries with competing strategic and economic interests could itself become a major achievement during its BRICS presidency, he said.Beyond geopolitical conflicts and disruptions to global supply chains, Kant said BRICS must also confront the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence as one of the biggest drivers of global change.“While there are conflicts that break down the supply chain, there's also the emergence of artificial intelligence as a very key driver for global growth and prosperity,” he said.The growing global competition around AI also makes it essential to establish frameworks for its responsible use, Kant added.
